queries: "Deep-Research Agents Can Be Poisoned via User-Generated Content"

sources_considered.why: Documents continuing AI content-farm pollution but does not attribute it to OpenAI Deep Research.
Product-specific testing documents factuality performance and provides a material qualification to simple extrapolation from other models.
Distinguishes OpenAI's product from other research agents and separates simulated attacks from actual public-web contamination.
Establishes the cited first version's May 22, 2026 availability.

evidence_items.locator: First criterion for inclusion in the AI Content Farm tracker
evidence_items.explanation: The tracker reports thousands of AI content-farm sites and describes their identification criteria. It does not identify which were produced with OpenAI Deep Research, so it cannot establish this product's contribution.

OpenAI's tests found factual errors but better factuality than the comparison models. This qualifies the proposed worsening mechanism: faster production does not by itself determine total pollution when error rates can differ.

evidence_items.publisher: arXiv; Tingwei Zhang, Harold Triedman, and Vitaly Shmatikov
evidence_items.explanation: The sampled OpenAI reports showed limited citation of user-generated content, unlike several other systems. The authors' poisoning experiments used other systems in simulation; they do not demonstrate Deep Research adding junk to the public web.

unresolved_gaps: No reviewed investigation traced an increase in public junk content specifically to OpenAI Deep Research.
No reviewed study established that the product's speed or expanded generation caused additional public pollution.
Several relevant medical-research studies could not be read with the required tool.
The poisoning preprint does not give an exact experimental date in the passages reviewed.
